Three parts. Part one: double quantum. A microwave field with two frequency components moves the NV spin between m_s = +1 and -1, and the +-1 superposition picks up phase twice as fast. The unpolarised 14N nucleus shifts each hyperfine manifold by Delta_m = m A, with A/2pi = 2.16 MHz, and a single rectangular pi pulse cannot serve all three. Part two: quantum signal processing. A sequence of K equal waits and N = K + 1 pulses is a polynomial of degree K in the detuning: the waits fix the degree, the pulse angles choose the polynomial. Part three: the DQ pi pulse with QSP. We write the target as a step function of the detuning, choose the wait time from the periodicity of the response, find the best achievable error for each number of pulses, and then turn to real pulses of finite length.

Part one sets up the physical problem: why double quantum, why the spin-1 behaves like a spin-1/2 under a balanced drive, how the unpolarised 14N enters, and why one rectangular pi pulse is not enough.

The double-quantum transition. The NV ground state is an electron spin S = 1 with zero-field splitting D = 2.87 GHz. A static field B along the NV axis splits m_s = +1 and -1 by 2 gamma B. In our set-up B = 44 mT (440 G), so 2 gamma B = 2.46 GHz and the two transitions sit at D - gamma B = 1.64 GHz and D + gamma B = 4.10 GHz. The diagram is not to scale. We apply one microwave field with two frequency components: omega_1 on the 0 <-> +1 transition and omega_2 on the 0 <-> -1 transition. Together they move the spin directly between +1 and -1: Delta m = 2, hence "double quantum" (DQ). Why bother: a superposition of +1 and -1 picks up the field-dependent phase of both levels, 2 gamma B t, while a single-quantum superposition of 0 and +1 picks up gamma B t (phases written in the frame rotating at D, so only the field-dependent part is shown). Twice the phase per unit field doubles the magnetometric sensitivity (Mamin et al., PRL 113, 030803 (2014)).

The rotating frame. Start in the laboratory frame. The NV ground state is a spin-1 with zero-field splitting D and Zeeman term gamma B S_z. The microwave field along x has two frequency components, with amplitudes B_1, B_2, frequencies omega_1, omega_2 and phases delta_1, delta_2. Go to the frame that rotates at omega_1 on |+1> and at omega_2 on |-1>. Every term that still oscillates at frequencies of order D or 2 gamma B is dropped: that is the rotating-wave approximation. What is left is time independent. The off-diagonal elements are the matrix elements of S_x, 1/sqrt2, times half the drive amplitude, gamma B_j / 2, with the phase of each component. This is Eq. (S3) of Mamin et al. The two diagonal entries are the detunings of each component from its own transition, Delta_1 = D + gamma B - omega_1 and Delta_2 = D - gamma B - omega_2. Their difference and their mean have different physics. S_z = diag(1, 0, -1) and S_z^2 = diag(1, 0, 1), so diag(Delta_1, 0, Delta_2) = Delta S_z + Delta_c S_z^2. The differential detuning Delta = (Delta_1 - Delta_2)/2 moves +1 and -1 in opposite directions: this is what the magnetic field does, and what the secular hyperfine interaction with the nucleus does. It is the signal in magnetometry, and the error we fight in this talk. The common-mode detuning Delta_c = (Delta_1 + Delta_2)/2 moves both levels together: a carrier away from D, temperature (D depends on temperature) and strain.

Why the spin-1 representation is natural. Start from the rotating-frame Hamiltonian of the previous slide and choose the two frequency components with equal amplitude, B_1 = B_2 = B_mw, mirrored phases delta_1 = phi and delta_2 = -phi, and no common-mode detuning. The off-diagonal elements become Omega_DQ / sqrt2 times e^{-i phi}, with Omega_DQ = gamma B_mw / 2, and these are exactly the matrix elements of Omega_DQ (cos phi S_x + sin phi S_y). So H-tilde is a spin-1 in an effective field: Delta along z and Omega_DQ in the equatorial plane at azimuth phi. Replace S by sigma/2 and you have h, a spin-1/2 in the same field. Three ways to see that the two evolve "the same way". First, two spin-1/2. Take two spin-1/2 particles and put them in the same field. Their total spin is S = s_1 + s_2, and one-half times one-half is one plus zero: the three symmetric states up-up, the symmetric combination, and down-down form a spin-1, the singlet is a spin-0. Our three levels are exactly that triplet: |+1> is up-up, |0> is the symmetric combination, |-1> is down-down. A Hamiltonian linear in S is the sum of the same h acting on each particle, h (x) 1 + 1 (x) h, so the evolution is u (x) u, each particle rotated by the same u, and it never leaves the triplet. The spin-1 evolution is u (x) u restricted to the triplet; this matrix is called D^1(u). The DQ transition, +1 to -1, flips both particles. Second, algebra. The spin-1 matrices S_x, S_y, S_z obey the same commutation relations as the Pauli matrices divided by two. A rotation is the exponential of a combination of generators, and the result of composing rotations depends only on these commutation relations. So the same generator exponentiates to "the same rotation", represented once by 2x2 and once by 3x3 matrices: e^{-i H-tilde t} = D^1(e^{-i h t}) for every Delta. D^1 maps products to products, so a whole sequence of pulses and free evolution acts on the NV as D^1(u), with u the evolution of the same sequence on a spin-1/2. Third, the classical picture. The expectation value of S obeys the same precession equation as a spin-1/2 Bloch vector, d<S>/dt = field x <S>. A spin-1 is a vector that rotates exactly like the spin-1/2 Bloch vector. Consequence: we can design pulses for a spin-1/2 and read off what they do to the NV. The correspondence needs one common field on both spin-1/2. It fails for a common-mode detuning (S_z^2 is an Ising coupling between the two particles), unequal amplitudes, and the transverse zero-field splitting E. With equal field per component the single-quantum Rabi frequency is Omega_SQ = sqrt2 Omega_DQ.

The DQ pi pulse in the spin-1/2 language. Write the spin-1/2 evolution with its Cayley-Klein parameters: P is the amplitude for the spin-1/2 to stay, Q the amplitude to flip, and |P|^2 + |Q|^2 = 1. D^1(u) is the triplet block of u (x) u, so every entry is a product of two spin-1/2 amplitudes. For example, the amplitude from |+1> = up-up to |-1> = down-down is Q times Q: both particles must flip. The amplitude to stay in |+1> is P times P. The middle entry, from |0> to |0>, is |P|^2 - |Q|^2. The DQ pi pulse exchanges |+1> and |-1>. That needs P = 0: every entry containing P vanishes, |+1> -> Q^2 |-1>, |-1> -> Q*^2 |+1>, and |0> -> -|0>. So the condition on the spin-1/2 is simply P = 0. All populations are polynomials in q = |Q|^2. From |0>: P_0 = (1 - 2q)^2 and P_(+-1) = 2q(1 - q). We will use this on the next slides: the |0> population tells us q. Finally D^1(-u) = D^1(u): u and -u are the same rotation, so the overall sign of u is invisible. Only Q^2 matters for a DQ target, and in particular the sign of Q is free.

The electron and the 14N nucleus. Natural nitrogen is 14N, nuclear spin I = 1. The full Hamiltonian of the electron spin S and the nuclear spin I: zero-field splitting D S_z^2, electron Zeeman gamma_e B S_z, the hyperfine interaction with a secular part A_par S_z I_z and a transverse part A_perp (S_x I_x + S_y I_y), the nuclear quadrupole P I_z^2, the nuclear Zeeman term -gamma_n B I_z, and the drive f(t), which couples to the electron and, about 10^4 times more weakly, to the nucleus. The sizes (Doherty et al., Phys. Rep. 528, 1 (2013)). A_par/2pi = -2.16 MHz: the only term comparable to the Rabi frequency; it shifts the electron transitions by A_par m_I. A_perp/2pi = -2.70 MHz, but it flips m_s and m_I together across gaps of order D +- gamma_e B, so it acts only in second order: shifts of about A_perp^2 / (D -+ gamma_e B), 4.5 kHz and 1.8 kHz at 44 mT, a thousand times smaller than A. The quadrupole, -4.95 MHz, and the nuclear Zeeman term, 135 kHz at 44 mT, are the same for every m_s, so they cancel in the electron transitions. The nuclear drive, about 7 kHz, is far off any nuclear resonance. Secular approximation: drop A_perp and the nuclear drive. Then H commutes with I_z, and in the eigenbasis |m> of I_z it is block diagonal: H = sum_m H_m (x) |m><m|. Each block is the electron alone, with the Zeeman term shifted by A_par m. The constant is P m^2 - gamma_n B m, a phase within each block. Each m defines a hyperfine manifold. The next slide writes H_m in the rotating frame. All of this assumes an unpolarised nucleus, p_m = 1/3. TODO (speaker to confirm): our field, 44 mT, is close to the excited-state level anticrossing (about 51 mT), where optical pumping polarises the 14N nucleus (Jacques et al., PRL 102, 057403 (2009)). If the nucleus is partly polarised in our set-up, the weights are not 1/3 and should be measured, for example from the three hyperfine resonances in pulsed ODMR.

H_m in the rotating frame. Take one block H_m and go to the same rotating frame as before. The common-mode detuning D - (omega_1 + omega_2)/2 does not depend on m and is set to zero. The differential detuning becomes Delta_m = Delta_0 + A_par m, where Delta_0 is the field detuning of the carrier pair, which we tune to zero on the m_I = 0 resonance. So each manifold is the same spin-1 in an effective field, with its own static detuning Delta_m: the 3x3 matrix above, which is Delta_m S_z + Omega_DQ (cos phi S_x + sin phi S_y), and its spin-1/2 image h_m. The sign convention: A_par is negative; we write A = |A_par| and Delta_m = m A, which does not matter because everything is symmetric in m. Because the blocks never mix, the whole evolution is block diagonal: U = sum_m D^1(u_m) (x) |m><m|, with u_m the spin-1/2 evolution of the sequence at detuning Delta_m. At room temperature the 14N is unpolarised: p_m = 1/3 each, a nuclear state diagonal in m. Trace out the nucleus, and the electron undergoes a mixed-unitary channel: with probability 1/3 it evolves with D^1(u_m). No electron-nuclear entanglement is created: for the electron the nucleus is a classical random label that selects one of three detunings, 0 and +-2.16 MHz. This is dephasing by a static distribution, not decoherence. No single carrier frequency removes all three detunings. So the design problem is: one sequence u, evaluated at three detunings, must do the right thing at all three.

The |0> population under DQ driving and its spectrum. Left figure: Omega/2pi = 10 MHz, Omega_DQ/2pi = 7.07 MHz, the drive on the m_I = 0 resonance; blue m_I = 0, red m_I = +-1 (Delta = +-2.16 MHz), dashed the average over the unpolarised nucleus, which is what a measurement of the |0> population sees. Why this shape. With phi = 0 the drive couples |0> only to one combination of +1 and -1, the bright state |B> = (|+1> + |-1>)/sqrt2, with strength Omega_DQ. The orthogonal combination, the dark state |D> = (|+1> - |-1>)/sqrt2, is not driven. The differential detuning couples bright and dark: S_z |B> = |D>, with strength Delta_m. So each manifold is a three-level ladder, |0> - |B> - |D>, a Morris-Shore reduction of the V system. On resonance, Delta = 0, the dark state is never reached and |0> and |B> exchange their population completely: P_0 = cos^2(Omega_DQ t). After the pi/2 pulse (Omega_DQ t = pi/2, 35 ns) |0> is empty, which is the preparation of the +-1 superposition; after the DQ pi pulse (Omega_DQ t = pi, 71 ns) the bright transition has made a full 2 pi rotation, the population is back in |0>, and +1 and -1 have been exchanged. Off resonance, the ladder has eigenvalues 0 and +-Omega', with Omega' = sqrt(Omega_DQ^2 + Delta^2). The state |0> has weight Delta^2/Omega'^2 on the zero eigenvector, which gives the closed form P_0 = [Delta^2/Omega'^2 + (Omega_DQ^2/Omega'^2) cos Omega' t]^2. It is the same as P_0 = (1 - 2q)^2 with Rabi's formula for the spin-1/2 flip probability, q = (Omega_DQ^2/Omega'^2) sin^2(Omega' t/2). The oscillation is faster (period 2 pi / Omega' = 135 ns for the outer manifolds, against 71 ns for m_I = 0 in P_0), and q never reaches 1: q is at most Omega_DQ^2/Omega'^2 = 0.91. So at the DQ pi time the outer manifolds return only to P_0 = ((Omega_DQ^2 - Delta^2)/Omega'^2)^2 = 0.69 (10 MHz drive): the rest is in |+-1>, partly in the dark state. Every second maximum is lower. |0> does empty (q = 1/2 is reached), which is why the preparation looks fine in population; its problem is the phase (next slide). The average over the nucleus contains three frequencies: 2 Omega_DQ from m_I = 0, and 2 Omega' and Omega' from the outer manifolds; the two fast lines beat at about A^2 / Omega_DQ. This is what two-frequency nutation looks like with an unpolarised 14N. The spectrum (right). Square the bracket: P_0 = a^2 + b^2/2 + 2ab cos(Omega' t) + (b^2/2) cos(2 Omega' t), with a = Delta^2/Omega'^2 and b = Omega_DQ^2/Omega'^2. So each manifold has at most two lines: one at 2 Omega' with weight Omega_DQ^4 / 2 Omega'^4, the bright-transition Rabi oscillation, and one at Omega' with weight 2 Delta^2 Omega_DQ^2 / Omega'^4, which exists only off resonance because it comes from the dark state. On resonance only the first survives, at 2 Omega_DQ, with weight 1/2. At Omega/2pi = 10 MHz: m_I = 0 gives a line at 14.14 MHz; m_I = +-1 give lines at 14.79 MHz and 7.39 MHz. Averaged over the nucleus (weights 1/3, 2/3) the amplitudes are 1/6 = 0.167 at 14.14 MHz, 0.279 at 14.79 MHz and 0.104 at 7.39 MHz. The coloured bars are these closed-form lines; the black curve is the Fourier amplitude of the averaged trace over 5 microseconds, which reproduces them. The two high lines are 0.65 MHz apart, about A^2/Omega_DQ, so a measurement must run for well over a microsecond to resolve them; doubling the drive halves that splitting and suppresses the line at Omega'.

One rectangular DQ pi pulse is not enough. The figure: one rectangular DQ pi pulse, Omega_DQ T = pi, in a manifold with detuning Delta. Rabi's formula for the spin-1/2 gives the flip probability q = (Omega_DQ^2 / Omega'^2) sin^2(Omega' T / 2), with Omega' = sqrt(Omega_DQ^2 + Delta^2); the DQ transfer |+1> -> |-1> is q^2, both spins must flip. The dots are the three hyperfine resonances, Delta = 0 and +-A. Three drives: the drive of Mamin et al., Omega_DQ/2pi = 31.25 MHz with a 16 ns pi pulse, and Omega/2pi = 20 MHz and 10 MHz, where Omega = sqrt2 Omega_DQ is the single-quantum Rabi frequency (Omega_DQ/2pi = 14.1 and 7.07 MHz). As the drive weakens, the profile narrows and the outer manifolds fall off. Expansion in eta_m = Delta_m / Omega_DQ: q = 1 - eta^2 + O(eta^4), so P_(-1) is about 1 - 2 eta^2, and the error is population left in |0>, P_0 about 2 eta^2. All errors are even in eta, so the average over the nucleus is 2/3 of the outer-manifold value: 1 - P_(-1) is about (4/3) eta_A^2, with eta_A = A / Omega_DQ. Exact values averaged over the nucleus: 6.3e-3 at the drive of Mamin et al. (eta_A = 0.069), 3.0e-2 at 20 MHz, 0.115 at 10 MHz (eta_A = 0.305); the process infidelities are 8.5e-3, 4.1e-2 and 0.15. A factor of about 20 between the drive of Mamin et al. and 10 MHz. The last column is the preparation, the pi/2 pulse that takes |0> into the +-1 superposition. It is insensitive in population: what stays in |0> is fourth order in eta, only 7e-7 at the drive of Mamin et al. and 2.6e-4 at 10 MHz. But the relative phase of the +-1 components is off by about 2 eta_m, with the sign of m_I: +-7.9 degrees, +-17.5 degrees and +-34.9 degrees in the outer manifolds. Averaged over the nucleus, a phase that depends on m shrinks the coherence. The preparation fails through its phase. Hence the requirement for part three. A requirement on populations alone is not enough for DQ sensing: the three manifolds must also acquire the same phase. In D^1(u) after a DQ pi pulse, |+1> -> Q^2 |-1>, so the phase that matters is that of Q^2. Phase coherence across the manifolds needs one common Q^2: Q(Delta_m) = s_m e^{i chi} with one chi for all three m. The signs s_m are free, because only Q^2 enters.

Part II: quantum signal processing, conceptually. First the simplest case: only waits, no pulses. Then we add pulses and ask what a sequence of K waits and N = K + 1 pulses can produce, Throughout, K is the number of waits, which is also the degree of the polynomials.

Start with the simplest sequence: no pulses at all, only K waits of length tau. During a wait only the detuning acts, so each wait is a rotation about z by the angle Delta tau: R_z(Delta tau) = exp(-i Delta tau sigma_z / 2). The clip draws them one after the other: R_z R_z R_z. Rotations about one axis add, so K waits are one rotation R_z(K Delta tau). In the basis up, down it is diagonal with entries z^{-K} and z^{K}, where z = e^{i theta} and theta = Delta tau / 2 is the half angle. So the stay amplitude is P = z^{-K} = e^{-i K theta}, and the flip amplitude is Q = 0. The animation: first the K blocks R_z(Delta tau) merge into one block R_z(K Delta tau). Once K is fixed, we plot the real and the imaginary part of P as functions of x = cos(Delta tau / 2). As Delta tau goes from 0 to 2 pi, x runs from 1 to -1. First K = 3, then K = 5. The real part is cos(K theta). As a function of x = cos theta this is a polynomial, the Chebyshev polynomial T_K(x): for K = 3 it is 4x^3 - 3x, for K = 5 it is 16x^5 - 20x^3 + 5x. The imaginary part is -sin(K theta) = -sin(theta) U_{K-1}(x), with the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind U_{K-1}, of degree K - 1: for K = 3, U_2 = 4x^2 - 1. So P is a polynomial of order K in x = cos(Delta tau / 2), plus sin(theta) times a polynomial of order K - 1. The order equals the number of waits. And x only sees cos(Delta tau / 2): a detuning and its negative give the same x.

Now insert pulses between the waits: N = K + 1 rotations about x, R_x(phi_1) to R_x(phi_N), with K = 3 waits in between. The clip starts with all angles at zero: that is the previous slide, Re P = T_3(x) and Q = 0. Then we turn the angles up one after another, to pi/2, 2 pi/3, pi/3 and pi/4, and at the end we move phi_2 down and back. Every frame is computed from the product of the 2 x 2 matrices. Watch two things. First, the curves change: the pulse angles choose what P and Q look like as functions of x. Second, they never get more wiggly than with three waits: Re P and Im Q stay polynomials of degree at most 3, Im P and Re Q are sin(theta) times polynomials of degree at most 2. The number of waits fixes the degree; the pulses only choose the coefficients. Unitarity holds at every frame: |P|^2 + |Q|^2 = 1. So turning a pulse moves weight between P and Q.

These are the polynomials that carry the rest of the talk. Left, the first kind: T_n(cos theta) = cos(n theta). T_0 = 1, T_1 = x, T_2 = 2x^2 - 1, up to T_5 = 16x^5 - 20x^3 + 5x. They all stay between -1 and +1 on [-1, 1], and T_n touches +1 and -1 alternately at n + 1 points. Right, the second kind: U_n(cos theta) = sin((n+1) theta) / sin theta. U_0 = 1, U_1 = 2x, up to U_4 = 16x^4 - 12x^2 + 1. They grow at the ends, up to n + 1 at x = +-1, because of the division by sin theta. The colours pair U_{n-1} with T_n: they are the imaginary and the real part of the same z^{-n}. Why they are polynomials: the identity cos(n+1)theta + cos(n-1)theta = 2 cos(theta) cos(n theta) gives the recurrence T_{n+1} = 2x T_n - T_{n-1}, and the same recurrence holds for U. Starting from T_0 = 1 and T_1 = x, every T_n is a polynomial of degree n. The physical reading of the recurrence: multiplying by x = cos theta moves harmonic n to n + 1 and n - 1. That is what one wait does to an amplitude. So each wait raises the degree by one. One identity we use later: T_n^2 + (1 - x^2) U_{n-1}^2 = 1, which is cos^2 + sin^2 = 1, the unitarity of the pulse-free sequence.

In general the pulses need not be about x. A quantum signal processing sequence: N instantaneous pulses G_1 to G_N, separated by K = N - 1 equal waits of length tau. Drawn here with N = 5 pulses and K = 4 waits; the bar heights stand for different pulse angles, and each pulse can also have its own phase, that is its own axis in the xy plane. Time runs left to right, the operator product right to left: u = G_N W G_{N-1} ... W G_1. The detuning enters only through the waits, W = R_z(Delta tau) = diag(z^{-1}, z) with z = e^{i theta}. That is the signal. The pulses are fixed rotations that do not depend on Delta; their angles and phases are the processing we design. Every wait multiplies an amplitude by z^{-1} or by z, and the pulses only mix the two amplitudes with constant coefficients. So the entries of u are polynomials in z and z^{-1} of degree K, the number of waits, with only the powers of the parity of K: z^{-K}, z^{-K+2}, ..., z^{K}. We write u in the standard SU(2) form with P on the diagonal and Q off the diagonal: P is the amplitude to stay, Q the amplitude to flip. This is the same pair as in Part I, where the DQ pi pulse is P = 0.

Now we want to know exactly what K waits and K + 1 pulses can produce. The cleanest way is to write the unitary in the Pauli basis and follow it through the sequence, one factor at a time. We take pulses about +x or -x. Any 2 x 2 unitary of determinant one can be written as u = A times the identity, minus i B X, minus i sin(theta) times (C Z + D Y). The factor sin(theta) is pulled out of the Z and Y parts on purpose. The wait is W = e^{-i theta Z} = x I - i sin(theta) Z, with x = cos(theta). A pulse about x is R_x(phi) = cos(phi/2) I - i sin(phi/2) X. The clip follows four pulses, angles pi/2, 2 pi/3, pi/3, pi/4, with three waits, and plots A, B, C, D as functions of x after every factor. - It starts with the first pulse alone: A = cos(phi_1 / 2) and B = sin(phi_1 / 2) are constants, C = D = 0. - One wait: the identity part of W multiplies everything by x. The Z part turns the identity into Z and X into Y, each with one factor sin(theta); and it turns Z and Y back into the identity and X with a factor sin^2(theta) = 1 - x^2. Written out: A goes to xA - (1 - x^2) C, B to xB - (1 - x^2) D, C to xC + A, D to xD + B. Every coefficient becomes a polynomial of one degree more, and every parity flips. The counter at the top goes up by one. - One pulse: since X commutes with I and X, and turns Z into Y, the pulse only rotates the pair (A, B) into itself and the pair (C, D) into itself, with the constant coefficients cos(phi/2) and sin(phi/2). The curves change shape, but the degrees do not. After three waits: A and B have degree at most 3 and are odd, C and D have degree at most 2 and are even. And the unitarity identity A^2 + B^2 + (1 - x^2)(C^2 + D^2) = 1 holds for every x; it is det u = 1. In the up/down basis the two entries are P = A - i sin(theta) C, the stay amplitude, and Q = -i B + sin(theta) D, the flip amplitude. The important part is the converse, the theorem of quantum signal processing: every set of real polynomials A, B, C, D with these degrees and parities that satisfies the unitarity identity is produced by some choice of K + 1 pulse angles about x. It was proven by Low, Yoder and Chuang (2016); the form with polynomials in x and the two parity classes is Theorem 1 of Martyn, Rossi, Tan and Chuang (2021), who write the pair as A - iB and C - iD. The count shows that nothing is left over. A, B, C, D together have 2(K + 1) real coefficients. The unitarity identity is one even polynomial of degree 2K, so it imposes K + 1 equations. That leaves K + 1 free numbers: exactly one angle per pulse. A useful consequence for design: any real function of x with the parity of K and modulus at most one can be realised as A, or with a pulse phase shift as B, of some sequence. So we pick one real polynomial and the rest follows. The pulses are then obtained from the polynomial by a finite algebraic procedure: complete the unitary, then strip one pulse and one wait at a time (Haah, Quantum 3, 190 (2019)). The waits fix the degree; the pulse angles choose the polynomials.

Part III. Part II showed that a sequence of instantaneous pulses and equal waits turns the detuning into a polynomial. Now we use that to design a phase-coherent DQ π pulse for the three ¹⁴N hyperfine manifolds. First we write down what the pulse must do at each detuning, then we choose the wait τ, and then we see why a straightforward expansion of the target is not good enough.

What the DQ π pulse has to do, detuning by detuning. The nucleus picks one of three detunings, Δ = mA with m = −1, 0, 1. Around each of them we allow a tolerance window of ±0.1A for slow field drifts: this is the passband, where the electron must be inverted, P = 0. For phase coherence Q must be the same up to a sign in all three windows: Q = s_m e^{iχ} with one common phase χ. The signs are free because only Q² enters the spin-1 operation; χ is free because shifting the phase of every pulse multiplies Q by a phase. Between the windows we want nothing to happen: the stopband, 0.3A to 0.7A and 1.3A to 1.5A in |Δ|, where Q = 0. The phase of P is left free there, because a detuning-dependent phase of P is just extra precession about z. Between passband and stopband there are transition bands of width 0.2A with no requirement: the response has to turn somewhere. Beyond 1.5A nothing is required. So the target is a step function of the detuning. The clip builds it: passband, transition bands, stopband, then the target |Q_t| (top) and |P_t| (bottom). How we measure the error. At one detuning we compare the spin-½ operation u that the sequence produces with the target operation u_t: ε(Δ) = 1 − |½ Tr u_t† u|² is zero when they agree and one when they are orthogonal, the process infidelity. The free phases (χ, and the phase of P in the stopband) are chosen to make it as small as possible. In the passband this gives |P|², the population that is not transferred, plus [Im(e^{−iχ} Q)]², the part of Q that has the wrong phase. In the stopband it gives |Q|², the population that is transferred although it should not be. Then E is simply the worst ε over the whole passband and stopband, the uniform error, and the design goal is E ≤ 10⁻³. For the spin-1 operation itself, the population error in the passband is about 2ε and the process infidelity (8/3)ε(1 − (2/3)ε). We do not use |Q − Q_t|² as the error: it is quadratic in the transfer error, so 10⁻³ would allow |P|² ≈ 0.06.

The waits carry the detuning, and a wait W = diag(e^{−iΔτ/2}, e^{iΔτ/2}) depends on Δ only through these two phases. If we shift Δ by 2π/τ, each phase moves by π, so every wait changes sign, W → −W. The sequence has K waits, so u → (−1)^K u, and Q² does not change at all. The spin-1 operation only sees Q², so the whole response is periodic in the detuning with period p = 2π/τ. The target has to live with that. Every window reappears at mA + np, its periodic images. An image landing on another window or in a transition band does no harm. But if an image lands in the stopband, the same detuning would have to be inverted and left alone at once. A window point and a stopband point differ by 0.2A to 0.8A, 1.2A to 1.8A or 2.2A to 2.6A, so τ is compatible exactly when no multiple of p falls into these ranges: 0.9A < p < 1.1A, 1.8A < p < 2.2A, or p > 2.6A. The clip: left, the circle z² = e^{iΔτ}, one turn per period of the response; green outer arcs are the windows, yellow inner arcs the stopband, red where a window lands on the stopband. Right, the detuning axis with the windows and their images. At p = A (τ = 2π/A = 463 ns) all three windows map to one point, z² = 1, and the stopband to the opposite side, around z² = −1. Sweeping to p = 3A, the three windows separate into three points with the stopband in between; red appears exactly in the gaps 1.1A < p < 1.8A and 2.2A < p < 2.6A. At p = 1.5A the image of the central window falls on the stopband at 1.5A, and the images of the outer windows on ∓0.5A: then 1 − r² ≤ E and r² ≤ E at one point, so E ≥ 1/2 for any number of pulses.

Instantaneous pulses, A/2π = 2.16 MHz, so 2π/A = 463.0 ns. τ = 2π/A needs N = 14 pulses (K = 13 waits). At π/A and 2π/3A the smallest degree is exactly two and three times larger, 27 and 40 pulses, with the same 6019 ns of free evolution: the best sequence is the 2π/A sequence with zero-angle pulses in between, every second or third pulse doing something. At 2π/4A and 2π/6A, 51 and 75 pulses give 5787 and 5710 ns, 4 and 5 % less free evolution, because the three windows are then separate points of the circle and part of the circle lies beyond 1.5A, where nothing is required. The incompatible values 2π/1.5A and 2π/2.5A stay at E = 0.50 for any number of pulses. So with instantaneous pulses τ = 2π/A is the natural choice: saving a few per cent of free evolution would cost four to five times as many pulses, and every real pulse adds its own duration and error.

Two targets are easy, and they show what the hard one asks for. Passband only, no stopband: with instantaneous pulses the target is the constant r ≡ ±1 = T_0, degree zero. One π pulse R_x(π) gives P = 0 and Q = −i at every detuning, exactly. Any further pulses in a design of this kind only serve to cancel the detuning dependence of the real, finite pulse. Exact at the three resonances only, Δ = 0 and ±A, with τ = 2π/A: then θ = Δτ/2 = πΔ/A, so θ_m = mπ and x_m = cos θ_m = (−1, 1, −1). The clip shows it: the three resonances move round the circle z = e^{iθ}; the central one stays at x = 1, the outer two both land on x = −1. With the signs (−, +, −) the conditions are r(1) = +1 and r(−1) = −1, and the straight line r = x = T_1 goes through both: degree K = 1, two pulses. Completing it gives the Ramsey-type sequence R_x(π/2) W R_x(π/2), with P = −i sin(Δτ/2) and Q = −i cos(Δτ/2): P = 0 and Q = ∓i at every Δ = nA. The figure on the right is |Q|² = cos²(πΔ/A) of that sequence. It inverts at every resonance, but in the stopband it transfers up to cos²(0.3π) = 0.35, and it is zero only at the single points ±0.5A and ±1.5A. Protecting the whole stopband is what costs pulses.

Two coordinates for the same function. In the Z basis every wait multiplies each path by z or z^{−1}, z = e^{iθ}, θ = Δτ/2, so Q is a Laurent polynomial in z of degree K with K + 1 coefficients. Since z^k + z^{−k} = 2 cos kθ = 2 T_k(x) and z^k − z^{−k} = 2i sin kθ = 2i sin θ U_{k−1}(x), the Laurent coefficients regroup into Chebyshev polynomials in x = cos θ: the same K + 1 numbers, a change of basis. The target is symmetric in the detuning: Q_t = −i r(θ) with r even, so q_k = q_{−k}. Then Σ q_k z^k = q_0 + Σ_{k>0} q_k (z^k + z^{−k}) = q_0 + Σ_{k>0} 2 q_k T_k(x): only cosines, a Chebyshev series in x. At τ = 2π/A, θ = πΔ/A, and the target lives on x ∈ [−1, 1]: the central window at x ≥ 0.951 (θ ≤ 0.1π), the outer windows both at x ≤ −0.951, the stopband at |x| ≤ 0.588. With the signs (−, +, −) the step is +1 near x = 1, 0 in the middle, −1 near x = −1, with the jumps in the middle of the transition bands, θ = 0.2π from the windows (x = ±0.809). Its Fourier cosine coefficients are a_k = (2/π) ∫ r(θ) cos kθ dθ = 4 sin(0.2πk)/(πk) for odd k, and zero for even k. With the signs (+, +, +) the same formula holds for the even k, with a_0 = 0.4. The figure shows the a_k: they fall only like 1/k (dashed envelope 4/(πk)), because the step has jumps. That is also why simply cutting this series after degree K does not work: next to each jump the cut series overshoots by about 9 % at every K (the Gibbs phenomenon), so after scaling it to |r| ≤ 1 the error stays near E ≈ 0.2 however many pulses we use. The series insists on reproducing the jump, which the target never asked for; a good polynomial uses the free transition bands instead, and that is the next slide.

From now on the flip amplitude of our sequences is Q = -i r with r real; I explain why on the slide after next. r is a Chebyshev series in x = cos(Delta tau / 2) whose degree K is the number of waits; N = K + 1 pulses. What does it mean to meet the target with error E? Read the three conditions one by one. In the passband we want full inversion with the right sign: the population left behind is |P|^2 = 1 - r^2, so asking s_m r >= sqrt(1 - E) means at most a fraction E stays behind, and since Q is purely imaginary the phase is automatically the same on all three windows. In the stopband we want nothing to happen: the transferred population is |Q|^2 = r^2, so |r| <= sqrt(E) means at most E is transferred. And everywhere |r| <= 1: that is all unitarity asks for, because given such an r the missing entry P can always be completed. For a fixed E all three are linear inequalities in the coefficients c_k. So we can ask a linear program: what is the smallest stopband bound on |r| we can reach while the passband and circle conditions hold? The best error E_N is where that bound equals sqrt(E). This is the best uniform approximation of the step, and no sequence of N instantaneous pulses can beat it: it is the upper bound of what QSP can do here. The clip shows the best approximation for N = 2, 4, up to 18 pulses at tau = 2 pi / A, plotted against Delta / A: green the passband, yellow the stopband, white the target. The curve flattens on the windows and on the stopband, and its error equioscillates. On the right, E_N on a log scale: 3.1e-2 at N = 6, 3.8e-3 at 10, 5.1e-4 at 14, 7.2e-5 at 18, a factor 7 to 8 per four pulses. One more pulse does not always help: N = 7 and 8 both give 1.9e-2, N = 15 and 16 give 2.3e-4 and 2.5e-4, because consecutive N alternate between the two sign patterns. The tolerance 1e-3 is first met at N = 14, that is K = 13 waits of 463 ns, about 6.0 microseconds; N = 13 gives 1.4e-3. Compare the cut Chebyshev series of the previous slide: it insists on the jump and stays at an error of about 0.2. The best approximation uses the free transition bands to turn smoothly, so its error falls exponentially.

From the best polynomial to the pulses. First the completion: 1 - r^2 is non-negative on the whole circle, so by the Fejér–Riesz theorem it is the squared modulus of a polynomial P of the same degree. That gives the full pair P, Q. Then layer stripping: the highest power of z in the pair is produced only by the last pulse, so its top coefficients fix that pulse; multiply it off together with one wait, and the degree drops by one. Repeat 13 times and the 14 angles come out. The top panel is the result, drawn in time order: N = 14 pulses, K = 13 waits. Bar height is the rotation angle in units of pi; up is a rotation about +x, down about -x; teal are the 13 free evolutions of tau = 2 pi / A = 463 ns. Nearly pi rotations at both ends, 0.983 pi; small rotations next to them; two 0.619 pi rotations in the middle. The sequence reads the same forwards and backwards: palindromic, which is the symmetry of the next slide. Bottom: Q of this sequence over |Delta| <= 5A. Because Q^2 repeats every 2 pi / tau = A, the sequence inverts at every Delta = nA, including the images at 2A to 5A outside the protected range, and leaves the state unchanged in between. Inside 1.5A, the pale blue region, that is exactly the target. Its error is 5.2e-4, slightly above the best value 5.1e-4, because the completion keeps a small margin below |Q| = 1. Free evolution 13 tau = 6019 ns.

Why can we work with one real function? The idea is symmetric quantum signal processing. In the QSP literature the pulses are written as a list of phase factors, and symmetric QSP restricts that list to a palindrome, phi_0, phi_1, ..., phi_1, phi_0. Dong, Meng, Whaley and Lin proposed it in 2021 as a way to compute phase factors by optimisation. Wang, Dong and Lin, in their 2022 paper on the energy landscape of symmetric QSP, showed two things. First, existence and uniqueness: for every admissible pair of polynomials, with the right degree, parity and normalisation, there is exactly one symmetric phase list that produces it. Second, the cost landscape: it has many global and local minima, yet optimisation from the fixed symmetric start (pi/4, 0, ..., 0, pi/4) robustly finds one particular solution, which they call the maximal solution; they prove that it lies close to that start and that the cost is strongly convex there when the target polynomial is small, of order one over the degree. Their convention has the signal as an x-rotation and the phases as z-rotations; ours is the same structure in the rotated basis, with waits about z and pulses about x, so a symmetric phase list is our palindromic pulse sequence. Here is the mechanism in our variables. The free evolution W = diag(e^{-i theta}, e^{i theta}) is diagonal, so it equals its transpose; a rotation about x is cos(theta/2) - i sin(theta/2) X, symmetric because X is. The transpose of a product reverses the order, and for a palindromic sequence the reversed product is the same product: u^T = u. In Cayley–Klein form that says the two off-diagonal entries are equal, Q = -Q*, so Q is purely imaginary at every detuning: Q = -i r with r real. Pulses about x alone also give Q(-Delta) = -Q(Delta)*, so r is even in theta: a cosine series, a real Chebyshev series in x of degree K with the parity of K. Two consequences. Phase coherence comes for free: every Q(Delta_m) is -i times a real number, so all three windows share the phase -pi/2 up to a sign, and only Q^2 matters for the DQ pi pulse. And the target becomes the three conditions on r we just saw. Nothing is lost by the restriction. For every error level the set of admissible Q is convex and invariant under the two maps Q(theta) -> Q(-theta) and Q -> -conj(Q(-theta)); averaging an admissible Q over them gives an admissible palindromic one. A check against the general convex program for a complex Q agrees to 3e-4 relative at N = 12 and 14, and training confirms it: at N = 14 the best symmetric and the best arbitrary sequences both reach 5.15e-4.

A real pulse has no polynomial description, so in practice the sequence is trained directly against the target. The loss is the mean error over a grid of M detunings: 30 points in each passband window and 40 in each stopband interval; M_pass of them are in the passband. Term by term. In the passband the operation we want is Q = ±e^{i chi}: full transfer with one common phase chi. The error at one detuning is 1 - [Re(e^{-i chi} Q)]^2. Because |P|^2 + |Q|^2 = 1, this splits into |P|^2, the population that was not transferred, plus [Im(e^{-i chi} Q)]^2, the part of Q with the wrong phase. In the stopband the operation is the identity, and the error is |Q|^2, the population that was transferred although it should not be. The common phase chi is free: shifting every pulse phase multiplies Q by a phase. So we minimise over chi in closed form. Using [Re(e^{-i chi} Q)]^2 = (|Q|^2 + Re(e^{-2 i chi} Q^2))/2, the sum over the passband is smallest when e^{-2 i chi} lines up with the sum of the Q_j^2, and that gives the modulus |sum Q_j^2|. Only Q_j^2 appears, so the signs s_m need not be chosen. Parameters: a symmetric sequence is fixed by the first half of its angles, ceil(N/2) of them, the sign choosing +x or -x; an arbitrary sequence has an angle and a phase for every pulse, 2N parameters. The gradient is exact: u is a product of 2x2 matrices, and one forward and one backward pass give the derivative with respect to every pulse. Two stages. Stage 1 minimises the mean L with a quasi-Newton method from 12 random starting points (also from the sequence obtained from the polynomial for arbitrary sequences, and from a fit to the best polynomial for symmetric ones). The mean optimum spreads the error unevenly, so stage 2 minimises the largest error over the grid directly, with the common phase fixed; finally E is evaluated on a dense grid. The figure: all 12 random starts at N = 14, symmetric. Thin lines are the mean error L during stage 1, thick lines the largest error so far during stage 2. Stage 1 takes L from 0.03–0.6 down to 1.6e-4, but the largest error is still about 1.8e-3; stage 2 trades mean for maximum and brings the largest error to 5.1e-4, the best achievable value, dashed, now equioscillating. Green runs reach it within 1 %: 7 of 12. Red runs stop in local minima, one with no inversion at all. Arbitrary sequences behave the same, 6 of 12, about seven times slower per run. The landscape of symmetric QSP is known to have many local minima (Wang, Dong and Lin 2022), which is why one uses several starts or a good one; from the polynomial's sequence or the fit, training converges in about 30 iterations. Over all N: from N = 3 on, the best trained symmetric and arbitrary sequences sit on the best achievable error; at N = 14 both reach 5.15e-4. At N = 2 training stops at 0.35 instead of 0.28: two pulses give Q = -i sin(theta) cos(theta), the mean error is lowest at a pi/2 rotation, and there the stage-2 step cannot move.

So far the pulses were instantaneous. A real rectangular pulse of amplitude Omega and phase phi lasting t is U = exp[-(i/2) t (Delta sigma_z + Omega(cos phi sigma_x + sin phi sigma_y))]: a rotation by t sqrt(Omega^2 + Delta^2) about an axis tilted out of the equator by arctan(Delta/Omega). It depends on the detuning, so the sequence is no longer a polynomial in z and no longer periodic in Delta. The clip, part one: a pi pulse on resonance takes the spin from up to down along a meridian. At Delta/Omega = 0.23 and 0.46 the axis tilts, and the spin misses the south pole. Inside our range of 1.5A, |Delta|/Omega_max reaches 0.46 at Omega/2pi = 10 MHz and 0.23 at 20 MHz; Omega_max = Omega/sqrt(2) in the spin-1/2 picture of the DQ drive. Far from resonance a pulse barely rotates the spin at all, so the periodic images of the windows are suppressed. Part two: to first order in Delta/Omega, a pulse of angle beta = Omega t equals the instantaneous pulse with a free evolution e = tan(beta/2)/Omega before and after it. The first-order terms match: in the frame of the pulse the term is (Delta/2 Omega)[sin beta sigma_z + (1 - cos beta) sigma_y]; for the instantaneous pulse between two free evolutions e it is (Delta e/2)[(1 + cos beta) sigma_z + sin beta sigma_y]; they agree for e = tan(beta/2)/Omega. In the clip, a pi/2 pulse at Delta/Omega = 0.46: the violet path is the real pulse; the teal path, instantaneous pulse then free evolution, ends next to it; the red point, the instantaneous pulse alone, is far off. For a small angle e is half the pulse duration; for beta -> pi it diverges, so a pi pulse cannot be replaced this way. So between pulses j and j+1 the free evolution is shortened to g_j = 2 pi/A - e_j - e_{j+1}, which keeps the effective spacing at 2 pi/A to first order. What remains is of relative size (Delta/Omega)^2 and grows with Delta. Example: the exact two-pulse design at tau = 2 pi/A, pi/2 - wait - pi/2, with real full-amplitude pi/2 pulses: tan(pi/4) = 1, so the wait is shortened by 2/Omega_max. Its population error is 1.4e-6 at the drive strength of Mamin et al. (Omega_DQ/2pi = 31.25 MHz) and 5.3e-4 at 10 MHz; without the shortening it is no better than one pi pulse (6.3e-3 and 0.11).

What happens if we simply play the trained N = 14 instantaneous design with real pulses, with the free evolutions shortened as on the previous slide, and do not retrain? Two pulse conventions. Fixed length: every pulse lasts t_p = 2 pi / Omega_max, 141 ns at 10 MHz and 71 ns at 20 MHz, and the angle is set by the amplitude. Full amplitude: every pulse is driven at Omega_max and lasts only as long as its angle requires. The errors: 8.0e-3 with full-amplitude pulses at 20 MHz, 7.9e-2 at 10 MHz, 0.17 with fixed-length pulses at 20 MHz, and 1.0 at 10 MHz, where a window is no longer inverted at all. Shortening the free evolution helps in three of the four cases, for example 8.0e-3 instead of 3.2e-2 at 20 MHz with full amplitude. The figure shows Im Q over |Delta| <= 5A, the black curve the instantaneous design. Three effects. The response is no longer periodic. The images of the windows are reduced, the more so the weaker the pulses: |Q| at 4A is 0.89 for full amplitude at 20 MHz, 0.25 at 10 MHz, and 0.05 for fixed-length pulses at 20 MHz. And inside 1.5A the distortion destroys the flat inversion and the flat stopband. So a finite-pulse sequence must be retrained.

Now retrain: the same loss and the same two stages, with the pulse angles and also the K = N - 1 free evolutions between the pulses as parameters, kept palindromic for symmetric sequences. Starting points: the trained instantaneous design with shortened free evolution; a continuation in the Rabi frequency, training at 160 MHz where the pulses are nearly instantaneous and stepping down to 10 MHz; and a few random starts. The table gives the smallest number of pulses N that meets the tolerance and the total duration. With full-amplitude pulses at 20 MHz, 14 pulses suffice, as with instantaneous pulses: 5.9e-4 symmetric, 9.4e-4 arbitrary, 5.9 microseconds. At 10 MHz it takes 15 (arbitrary, 6.4 microseconds) or 16 pulses (symmetric, 6.7 microseconds). So full-amplitude real pulses cost 0 to 2 extra pulses. Fixed-length pulses are much harder: 19 at 20 MHz and 21 at 10 MHz, and no arbitrary sequence up to 18 pulses. Why fixed length is hard: a fixed-length pulse with a small angle is a weak pulse, Omega_k = a_k Omega_max, so |Delta|/Omega_k is large and the distortion strong; a full-amplitude pulse is always driven at Omega_max and lasts only as long as its angle requires. Unlike with instantaneous pulses, arbitrary phases sometimes help: 15 instead of 16 at 10 MHz. The figure shows the error of the retrained symmetric sequences as a function of N against the best achievable error with instantaneous pulses, grey. The curves are not monotone because training is a local search from a few starting points: they are upper bounds on what N real pulses can do. One more trick: put one or two extra pulses into every period, spacing pi/A or 2 pi/3A, and retrain everything. At 10 MHz with full-amplitude pulses this gives 5.2e-4 in 5.9 microseconds; with fixed-length pulses 7.7e-4 in 5.8 microseconds and 2.6e-4 in 6.4 microseconds. These are the shortest 10 MHz designs. With instantaneous pulses the extra pulses would be useless; with real pulses they give the training the freedom to cancel the detuning dependence of the pulses.

The second operation a DQ magnetometer needs: prepare the superposition of plus one and minus one from zero, B_phi = (|+1> + e^{i phi} |-1>) / sqrt2. The sequence acts as D^1(u), and the prepared state is the middle column of D^1(u): minus sqrt2 P Q-star, |P|^2 - |Q|^2, sqrt2 Q P-star. So the populations of plus and minus one are always equal, and the relative phase is phi = pi + 2 arg(Q P-star). The magnetometer reads the DQ coherence. With the nucleus mixed it is the average over the three manifolds, minus two thirds times the sum of (P_m Q_m-star)^2. It reaches its maximum 1/2 only if every manifold has |P_m|^2 = 1/2 and the same phase. Correct populations with phases that differ between the manifolds average the coherence away. So the requirement is phase coherence: the same state in all three manifolds. The target: a pi/2 pulse about x, P = 1/sqrt2 and Q = -i/sqrt2, on every window of plus-minus 0.1A. That prepares B_0. Every other phase follows from the same design: advancing the phase of every pulse by phi_0 multiplies Q by e^{i phi_0}, so phi goes to phi + 2 phi_0, exactly, for pulses of any shape. The state depends on P and Q only up to a common phase, so the clip shows them with that phase chosen to make P real. First the target bars on the three windows: P = 1/sqrt2, Re Q = 0, Im Q = -1/sqrt2. Then one rectangular pi/2 pulse at Omega/2pi = 10 MHz, 35 ns. It moves the population correctly, P stays at 1/sqrt2, but Re Q tilts with the detuning: the prepared phase turns by about 2 Delta / Omega_DQ. A real pulse acts like an instantaneous pulse between two short free evolutions, and the free evolution after it turns the phase. Infidelity 0.09 at plus-minus A, 6.0e-2 averaged over the nucleus, and the coherence drops from 0.5 to 0.44. At the drive of Mamin et al. the same error is 3.2e-3, at 20 MHz 1.5e-2. Then the robust design: four fixed-length pulses about plus and minus x, no waits, 566 ns at 10 MHz. P, Re Q and Im Q are flat across all three windows, infidelity at most 8.8e-5. At 20 MHz three pulses suffice, 212 ns. The full Hamiltonian check: electron and nitrogen, counter-rotating terms, the cross terms of the two frequency components, non-secular couplings, nucleus mixed, all transitions detuned together by up to 0.2 MHz. At 10 MHz this design stays between 4.1e-5 and 1.5e-4, coherence 0.5000. At 20 MHz a detuning-independent leakage of about 7e-4 remains. The time-reversed sequence reads the state out exactly, because P^2 + Q^2 = 0 for a phase-coherent preparation.

In the polynomial picture the preparation is the easy case. On every window the target is the same pair, P = 1/sqrt2 and Q = -i/sqrt2. A sum of equal steps over the three windows is a constant: degree zero, one coefficient. With instantaneous pulses a single pi/2 pulse is exact at every detuning, and the best achievable error is zero for any number of waits; the same holds for any pulse shape. So the pulses of a robust design are there only to cancel the detuning dependence of the real pulses, and waits, which separate the manifolds, only lengthen the sequence. That is why the shortest robust designs have no waits: 566 ns with fixed-length pulses at 10 MHz against 1324 ns with waits of 2 pi / 3A, and 145 ns at full amplitude. The target becomes a genuine step only with a stopband: if zero must also be left unchanged at other detunings within 3A, for instance a second NV orientation or a carbon-13 split line, with transition bands of 0.2A. Then |P| must be 1/sqrt2 on the windows and 1 in the stopband. Take tau = 2 pi / 6A, 77 ns, the longest tau whose period covers |Delta| <= 3A without images of the windows. Left: |P| of the best approximation for N = 7, 12, 23 and 46 pulses, the target green on the windows and amber on the stopband. With 7 pulses the response only sketches the three dips; with 12 and 23 they sharpen; with 46 pulses, 45 waits and 3.47 microseconds of free evolution, the error falls below the tolerance, 8.2e-4. Middle: the Chebyshev coefficients of r_z = |P|^2 - |Q|^2 in cos(Delta tau). The target's coefficients, crosses, decay only like 1/j, modulated by the array factor 1 + 2 cos(j A tau) of the three windows. The best approximations follow the low coefficients and drop far below the target's at high index: they use the transition bands instead of reproducing the jump. Right: the best achievable error as a function of N. Up to six pulses it stays near 0.5: a polynomial of such low degree cannot be close to 1/sqrt2 on the windows and to 1 in the stopband at once. Then it falls roughly exponentially and meets 1e-3 at N = 46. Time-symmetric sequences need 49. Any pulse shape needs at least 3.33 microseconds. Robust: hundreds of nanoseconds; with a stopband: microseconds.

Three sequences, all with pulses about plus or minus x, at Omega/2pi = 10 MHz, where Omega_DQ/2pi = 7.07 MHz. Top, exact at the three resonances: three fixed-length pulses of 141 ns with two waits of 2 pi / 3A, 154 ns: 1.29 pi, 1.41 pi, 1.80 pi, all about plus x, 733 ns. Three pulses because there are three conditions: one real equation at Delta = 0 and two at +A; minus A follows by symmetry. With one pulse fewer, or with a palindromic three-pulse sequence, there is no solution. It is exact at the centres of the windows only. At 20 MHz it takes 521 ns, at the drive of Mamin et al. 405 ns. Middle, robust over the windows, no waits: four fixed-length pulses, 0.34 pi about x, 1.75 pi about minus x, 1.07 pi about x, 1.16 pi about minus x, 566 ns. This is the design of the clip. Bottom, robust, no waits, full amplitude: each pulse is driven at the full Rabi frequency and lasts only as long as its angle requires: 0.33 pi, 0.77 pi about minus x, 0.95 pi, 145 ns in total, worst infidelity 2.8e-4 on the windows. At 20 MHz the same kind of design takes 134 ns. A robust preparation thus takes about 0.13 to 0.57 microseconds.

A different kind of target: the universal NOT. The ideal universal NOT maps every pure state to the orthogonal one, it inverts the Bloch vector; that map is antiunitary, and no physical operation does it. The best channel that treats all inputs alike contracts and inverts, r goes to -r/3, with fidelity 2/3 for every input: one third of the sum of sigma_j rho sigma_j (Buzek, Hillery and Werner, Phys. Rev. A 60, R2626, 1999). The unpolarised nucleus provides the average. Each manifold gets its own unitary U_m, and the electron sees one third of the sum of U_m rho U_m-dagger. For equal weights this is the universal NOT exactly when the three Bloch rotations sum to minus the identity: all three angles must be pi and the three axes orthonormal. The frame and a sign per manifold are free. In P and Q, a pi rotation about n has P = -i n_z and Q = n_y - i n_x. So on window m the target is a different pair. This is the only target in this talk that differs between the windows: for orthogonal axes two window targets are sqrt2 apart, genuine steps. Here the single-frequency qubit, zero and minus one, where u is the qubit operation. The clip: first the target bars, real part blue and imaginary part orange, in the frame the design uses. Re P = 0 on every window because every rotation is a pi rotation. Then the robust design: eight fixed-length pulses at Omega/2pi = 20 MHz with seven waits of 2 pi / 3A, 1480 ns. Each component follows its bar across the window and turns between the windows. Process infidelity at most 6.9e-4 on every window. At tau = 2 pi / 3A the three resonances sit at the cube roots of unity on the circle of the waits, as far apart as possible. There is even a closed form with instantaneous pulses: a pi pulse about x, a wait, a pulse about y by beta with cos beta = 1/3, a wait. A palindromic sequence cannot do it: it has Q purely imaginary, n_y = 0 on every window, and three orthogonal axes cannot all lie in the x-z plane. What it shows: 2/3 is also what measure-and-prepare reaches, and the channel is entanglement breaking. Each pi rotation squares to -1, so applying the sequence twice restores the input. With the nucleus unpolarised this demonstrates control, three different rotations from one sequence; a quantum test would need the nitrogen in a superposition of m_I.

How close can QSP get to this step target? With K waits, P and Q are Laurent polynomials of degree K in z = e^{i Delta tau / 2}. Single-frequency qubit, tau = 2 pi / 3A. Left: one component of the rotation axis, n_x = -Im Q, of the best uniform approximation for N = 2, 4 and 8 pulses; the green bars are the targets in the frame x, y, z on the windows at -A, 0, +A. With two pulses, one harmonic pair, the response passes the targets with steep slopes; with four it reaches them near the centres but slopes across the windows; with eight it is flat on each window and turns in the transition bands. Middle: the coefficient norms of the target, extended across each gap by a step at the gap centre, in harmonics of e^{i Delta tau}. At this tau the three windows are thirds of the circle, and harmonic j carries the component j mod 3 of the three-point Fourier transform of the window values: zero for j a multiple of 3, otherwise 3 / (2 pi |j|), in every frame. So they decay only like 1/j. The best approximation with K = 8 waits does not follow these coefficients: its constant term is 0.74 instead of 0.58, and it uses the third harmonic, which the step lacks. Right: the worst process infidelity on the windows as a function of K. The cut series, grey, overshoots at every degree and stays between 0.05 and 0.33: the Gibbs phenomenon. Smoothing the steps with a Gaussian restores convergence, orange, but needs K = 22 waits. The best approximation, blue, is a lower bound for every sequence of K + 1 instantaneous pulses: it falls in steps, 0.34 at K = 1, 3.9e-2 at K = 3, 1.3e-2 at K = 6, then by a factor 30 to 4.3e-4 at K = 7. So no sequence of fewer than 8 instantaneous pulses meets the tolerance, and 8 suffice: a sequence refined from the search reaches 5.8e-4. For any pulse shape the bound gives at least 886 ns. A shorter tau trades waits for time at nearly constant total: 12 waits and 926 ns at 2 pi / 6A, 48 and 889 ns at tau A / 2 pi = 0.04. Tau near pi / A is excluded: two windows coincide modulo the period. The two-frequency DQ qubit needs at least 9 pulses and 905 ns.

Single-frequency qubit, Omega/2pi = 20 MHz is the Rabi frequency of the one microwave field, every pulse 50 ns long with free amplitude and phase, waits of 2 pi / 3A = 154 ns. Top, exact at the three resonances: four pulses, 663 ns; 1.13 pi at 0 degrees, 0.48 pi at 100, 1.85 pi at 250, 0.70 pi at 259. With finite pulses four are needed: with three the residual stays at 8e-3 to 3.4e-2. At 10 MHz the exact design takes 863 ns, at 40 MHz 563 ns. Exact designs are sensitive to a common detuning: 2.7e-2 at 0.1 MHz. Bottom, each rotation robust on its window: eight pulses, 1480 ns, the design of the clip. But per-rotation robustness is not the right target for the channel: the process infidelity is second order in an axis error, while the channel's transfer matrix is first order in it, and a field drift detunes all three transitions together. These designs miss the channel by 1.4 to 1.5e-2. Middle, the channel kept at the universal NOT for every common detuning up to 0.1A: seven pulses, 1276 ns, and 1.3e-4 at a 0.1 MHz detuning. With quasi-static dephasing, T2-star = 1 microsecond: 5.1e-2 for the exact design, 2.7e-4 for this one. No design tolerates a 2 percent amplitude error: 2.1 to 7.4e-2. Without waits, a composite pulse of 10 pulses at 10 MHz or 20 at 20 MHz takes 1000 ns, 13 percent above the 886 ns bound. The two-frequency DQ qubit needs five pulses for the exact design, 1324 and 971 ns. With the full nine-level Hamiltonian, checked at 24.1 mT, the exact designs invert every cardinal input with fidelity 0.664 to 0.669, and a second application recovers every input to at least 0.9987; the channel-robust design deviates by 1.1e-3. Four synchronised frequency-selective pi pulses would take 1.6 to 5.5 microseconds and still leave 7.8e-3 to 7.6e-2.

Four points to take home. First, the problem. The DQ pi pulse we need acts on a mixed, detuned spin: the nitrogen is unpolarised, so with probability one third each it shifts the transition by -A, 0 or +A, and the electron undergoes the average of three different unitaries. One pulse cannot be right for all three. Second, the tool. QSP turns a sequence of waits and pulses into a Laurent polynomial in z, equivalently a Chebyshev polynomial in x = cos(Delta tau / 2), and the pulse angles tune its coefficients. The best polynomial approximation of the target is the upper bound on what N pulses can achieve, and any good sequence reaches it. So the real design work is in setting the target function: which detunings must be inverted, which must be left alone, and which are free. Third, the free evolution tau is not a free parameter. It decides where the three windows sit on the circle and where their periodic images land; at tau = 2 pi / A all three windows map to one point, and 14 pulses meet the tolerance with 6.0 microseconds of free evolution. In the gaps between compatible values the target cannot be met at all. Fourth, real pulses depend on the detuning, break the periodicity and must be retrained. With full-amplitude pulses that costs no extra pulse at 20 MHz and one or two at 10 MHz.

Backup: the Pauli form of a sequence of instantaneous pulses about plus or minus x, written without choosing a basis: u = A 1 - i B X - i sin theta (C Z + D Y), with A and B real polynomials in x of degree at most K, the number of waits, and the parity of K, C and D of degree at most K - 1 and the parity of K - 1, and A^2 + B^2 + (1 - x^2)(C^2 + D^2) = 1, which is det u = 1. Dictionary: reading the same operator in the two bases. In the Z basis, P = <up|u|up> = A - i sin theta C and Q = <down|u|up> = -iB + sin theta D. In the ± basis of X, P_± = <+|u|+> = A - iB, and <-|u|+> = -i sin theta Q_± with Q_± = C - iD. The operators never change, only their matrices: X is diagonal and Z off-diagonal in the ± basis. Induction. One pulse R_x(phi) = c 1 - i s X is K = 0: A = c, B = s, C = D = 0. A wait W = x 1 - i sin theta Z maps (A, B, C, D) to (xA - (1 - x^2)C, xB - (1 - x^2)D, A + xC, B + xD): the {1, X} block goes into itself times cos theta and into {Z, Y} times sin theta, and {Z, Y} comes back through sin^2 theta = 1 - x^2. Degrees rise by one and parities flip. A pulse R_x(phi) maps (A, B, C, D) to (cA - sB, cB + sA, cC + sD, cD - sC): it keeps the two blocks apart. Symmetries. W(-Delta) = X W(Delta) X and X R_x X = R_x, so u(-Delta) = X u(Delta) X; in the Z basis P(-Delta) = P(Delta)* and Q(-Delta) = -Q(Delta)*, i.e. P has real Laurent coefficients and Q imaginary ones. For a palindromic sequence u^T = u, so Q is purely imaginary, D = 0, and Q = -i B(x), a real Chebyshev series. Pulses about general equatorial axes break both symmetries; that is generalized QSP (Motlagh and Wiebe, PRX Quantum 2024).

Backup: u = W R_x(phi) W multiplied out in both bases, with c = cos(phi/2), s = sin(phi/2), x = cos theta. Z basis: diag(z^{-1}, z) times [[c, -is], [-is, c]] times diag(z^{-1}, z) = [[c z^{-2}, -is], [-is, c z^2]]. So P = c z^{-2}, Q = -is, and unitarity is c^2 + s^2 = 1 at once. ± basis: R_x(phi) = diag(e^{-i phi/2}, e^{i phi/2}) and W = [[x, -i sin theta], [-i sin theta, x]]. P_± is the sum of two paths, stay-stay, cos^2 theta e^{-i phi/2}, and flip-flip, (-i sin theta)^2 e^{i phi/2}: P_± = (cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta) cos(phi/2) - i (cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta) sin(phi/2) = c T_2(x) - is. The one-flip paths give <-|u|+> = -i sin theta cos theta (e^{-i phi/2} + e^{i phi/2}) = -i sin theta · 2cx, so Q_± = c U_1(x). Unitarity: |P_±|^2 + (1 - x^2)|Q_±|^2 = c^2 T_2^2 + s^2 + (1 - x^2) c^2 U_1^2 = c^2 [T_2^2 + (1 - x^2) U_1^2] + s^2 = c^2 + s^2 = 1, using T_n^2 + (1 - x^2) U_{n-1}^2 = cos^2 n theta + sin^2 n theta = 1. In the Pauli form: A = c T_2, B = s, C = c U_1, D = 0, as it must be for a palindromic sequence. And q = |Q|^2 = s^2 at every Delta: waits next to a Z preparation or readout only add phases. Here the Laurent form is the simpler one.

Backup: the first designs targeted only the three resonances, Delta = 0 and ±A, at tau = 2 pi / 3A = 154 ns. For pulses about ±x, P(-Delta) = P(Delta)*, so P(0) = 0 is one real condition and P(A) = 0 two; a palindromic sequence has Q purely imaginary, so the inversion is phase-coherent. Three independent angles therefore need a palindromic sequence of five pulses with four free evolutions. They were found by least squares from many random starts. Durations: 777, 971 and 1324 ns at the drive of Mamin et al. (Omega_DQ/2pi = 31.25 MHz), 20 MHz and 10 MHz with fixed-length pulses of free amplitude; 646, 683 and 747 ns with full-amplitude pulses. One pi pulse has a population error of 6.3e-3, 3.0e-2 and 0.11 at these drives. In the full nine-level laboratory-frame model with the nucleus unpolarised, the population error goes from 0.11 for one pi pulse to 3.1e-4 for the design at 10 MHz, and from 3.0e-2 to 8.3e-4 at 20 MHz. The rotating-frame model predicts zero; the remainder grows with the length of the sequence. The figure: population error as a function of a common detuning at 10 MHz (left) and 20 MHz (right), the five-pulse design in violet, one pi pulse in grey. The designs vanish at the three resonances but rise steeply between them, because they are constrained only at three points. That is what motivated the target over tolerance windows in the main part.

Backup: an earlier version of the target asked for the identity on the whole range |Delta| <= 3A outside the windows and transition bands, at tau = 2 pi / 6A = 77 ns, so that one period of Q^2 covers |Delta| <= 3A. Best uniform approximations: an error of 0.1 needs 36 instantaneous pulses, 2.7 microseconds of free evolution; 1e-2 needs 68, 5.2 microseconds; 1e-3 needs 104, 7.9 microseconds. Compare 14 pulses and 6.0 microseconds for the narrower stopband of the main part. The smallest degree K that meets the tolerance falls roughly as 1/tau, while the total free evolution K tau stays between 5.9 and 6.8 microseconds for every tau: at 2 pi / 3A the smallest degree is 39, at least 5.9 microseconds for any pulse shape. The step target written as a Laurent series in w = e^{i Delta tau} and smoothed across the bands needs degree 48 instead of 21 at 2 pi / 3A, and 109 instead of 41 at 2 pi / 6A: it fixes the shape inside the bands, which the best approximation chooses freely. The figure: the target, minus one, plus one, minus one on the windows and zero outside, with the best approximations for N = 17, 39 and 104 pulses.

Backup: continuation in the Rabi frequency. The instantaneous sequence is first trained at Omega/2pi = 160 MHz, where the pulses are nearly instantaneous, and then retrained at 80, 40, 28, 20, 16, 13, 11.5 and 10 MHz in turn, each time from the previous optimum with the pulse centres kept in place. The figure: for the N = 14 symmetric sequence the error rises smoothly from 5.2e-4 at 160 MHz to 1.5e-3 at 10 MHz with full-amplitude pulses, but to 2.0e-2 with fixed-length pulses, most of the rise between 40 and 16 MHz. Finite-pulse training needs several hundred iterations, more than with instantaneous pulses, and of 524 runs 39 stopped without any inversion. The table: one or two extra pulses in every period of the N = 14 symmetric design, spacing pi/A (27 pulses) or 2 pi/3A (40 pulses), with everything retrained at 10 MHz. Full amplitude: 1.5e-3 becomes 5.2e-4 at the same duration of about 5.9 microseconds. Fixed length: 1.4e-2 becomes 7.7e-4 in 5.8 microseconds and 2.6e-4 in 6.4 microseconds, the shortest 10 MHz designs found. With instantaneous pulses the extra pulses would be useless, because the optimum is a function of z^n; with real pulses they give the training the freedom to cancel the detuning dependence of the pulses.

Backup: how many pulses a step with a gap needs. For the sign function with a gap of width Delta theta, a polynomial of degree K proportional to ln(1/epsilon)/Delta theta reaches uniform error epsilon (Low and Chuang 2017; Martyn et al. 2021). Here the gap is the transition band, 0.2A in Delta, which is Delta theta = 0.2 pi at tau = 2 pi / A and 0.2 pi / 6 at tau = 2 pi / 6A. The plot shows the number of pulses N as a function of log10(1/E). Violet: the target of the main part at tau = 2 pi / A, E_N at N = 6, 10, 14, 18 (3.1e-2, 3.8e-3, 5.1e-4, 7.2e-5): a straight line, the error falls geometrically, a factor 7 to 8 per four pulses. Grey: the wider stopband over |Delta| <= 3A at tau = 2 pi / 6A, N = 36, 68, 104 at E = 8.7e-2, 8.8e-3, 9.4e-4: also linear in ln(1/E). From the slopes, the constant c = K Delta theta / ln(1/epsilon) is about 1.2 at tau = 2 pi / A and about 1.6 at tau = 2 pi / 6A: the same order, although the second target has three windows and six bands per period.
